content:
The largest possible sum is \(78\), but \(S=\{1,\dots,12\}\) has a valid partition, e.g.
\[
\{12,11,10,6\},\quad \{1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9\}
\]
both sum to \(39\), so \(78\) is not allowed.

Next largest sum is \(77\), which forces
\[
S=\{2,3,\dots,12\}.
\]
Since \(77=7\cdot 11\), the only possible \(k\ge 2\) are \(7\) and \(11\).

- If \(k=7\), each part must sum to \(11\). With \(11\) elements in \(7\) nonempty parts, at least \(3\) parts would have size \(1\), so we would need at least three copies of \(11\), impossible.
- If \(k=11\), each part must sum to \(7\), so every part would have to be the singleton \(\{7\}\), impossible.

Thus \(\{2,\dots,12\}\) has no equal-sum partition, so the maximum possible sum is
\[
\boxed{77}.
\]
